hook: The quiet painter of Delft, master of light, who left only about 35 pictures.

pages.x: Johannes Vermeer was born in Delft in 1632. His father wove silk, kept an inn and dealt in paintings. Almost nothing is known about how he trained. At 21 he married Catharina Bolnes and joined the painters' guild.

A maid pours milk into a bowl in a quiet kitchen, light falling through a window. Vermeer painted slowly, perhaps two or three pictures a year, using costly ultramarine blue made from crushed lapis lazuli.
He painted his town from across the river, sunlight breaking over the roofs after a shower. The French writer Proust called it the most beautiful painting in the world.

A girl turns to look at us over her shoulder, in a blue and yellow turban, with a large pearl at her ear. She is not a portrait of anyone in particular but a study of a face. She has been called the Mona Lisa of the North.
Some think he used a camera obscura, a dark box with a lens that throws an image onto a screen, because of the soft glints and blurs of light in his pictures. No one knows for sure.

He had 15 children, 11 of whom survived. When war ruined the art market in 1672, he sank into debt and despair, and died in 1675 at 43. His widow gave two of his paintings to the baker to pay the bread bill.

He was forgotten for two centuries. In the 1940s a forger, Han van Meegeren, sold a fake Vermeer to the Nazi leader Hermann Göring. Charged with treason for selling a national treasure, he proved it was a fake by painting another "Vermeer" in front of witnesses.
Vermeer is the great painter of light and quiet moments. Only about 35 of his paintings survive, but they are among the most loved in the world.
